prompt: What share of the data lies inside a boxplot's box?

choices.text: A quarter
choices.why: A quarter lies on each side of the median inside the box, so the box holds two quarters.

choices.text: Everything except the outliers
choices.why: That is the box and the whiskers together.

choices.text: Three quarters
choices.why: Three quarters lie below Q3, not inside the box.

choices.text: Half of it, from Q1 to Q3
choices.why: Right. From Q1 to Q3 is the middle half.

prompt: A region's quartiles are 25.8 and 39.0 minutes. Where is its upper fence, in minutes, to one decimal place?
hint: Q3 plus one and a half times the box length.

prompt: Why did the upper whisker stop at 57.3 minutes when the slowest delivery took 101.3?

choices.text: 57.3 was the last value inside the fence
choices.why: Right. Values beyond 59.05 are drawn as separate points.

choices.text: Whiskers always stop at the 95th percentile
choices.why: Some software does that, but Tukey's rule is the fence.

choices.text: 101.3 was removed as an error
choices.why: It is still drawn, as a point of its own.

choices.text: The axis ended at 60
choices.why: The axis ran past 100 to show the slowest delivery.

prompt: In a box, the median sits near the left edge and the right whisker is much longer than the left. What does the distribution look like?

choices.text: Symmetric
choices.why: A symmetric box has its median near the middle and even whiskers.

choices.text: Skewed right
choices.why: Right. A long tail of high values pulls the upper parts out.

choices.text: Skewed left
choices.why: That would put the long whisker on the left.

choices.text: Bimodal
choices.why: A box cannot show two peaks at all.

prompt: Two groups have identical boxplots. What can you conclude about their data?

choices.text: That their distributions are the same
choices.why: One had a single peak and the other two clusters.

choices.text: That they have the same number of values
choices.why: A box says nothing about the count.

choices.text: That neither has outliers
choices.why: Outliers would show; but the rest of the shape would not.

choices.text: Only that they share five numbers
choices.why: Right. Group A and group B shared a box and nothing else.

prompt: Group B's median was 30, and no value lay between 26 and 34. How can the median be a value nobody had?

choices.text: The box was drawn wrongly
choices.why: The box is correct; the summary is what misleads.

choices.text: Medians are rounded to the nearest ten
choices.why: Nothing was rounded.

choices.text: With an even count it is the average of the two middle values
choices.why: Right. Those were 26 and 34.

choices.text: Outliers moved the median
choices.why: Group B had no outliers, and medians resist them anyway.

prompt: A box rests on 6 values and the box beside it on 600. What should the chart add?

choices.text: A thicker outline for the larger group
choices.why: A reader would not know what thickness means.

choices.text: The count beside each box
choices.why: Right. Boxes look alike whatever their size.

choices.text: Nothing; boxes already show the count
choices.why: They do not, which is the point.

choices.text: A pie of the two counts beneath
choices.why: Writing the two numbers is simpler and exact.

prompt: What does a violin plot show that a boxplot does not?

choices.text: The shape, such as a second peak
choices.why: Right. It is a mirrored density curve.

choices.text: The exact count of values
choices.why: Violins hide the count too.

choices.text: The quartiles to two decimal places
choices.why: Exact numbers are not what a violin is for.

choices.text: Each value as its own dot
choices.why: That is a strip plot.

prompt: Which of the three views is most honest for a group of 20 deliveries?

choices.text: A strip of every point
choices.why: Right. Twenty dots hide nothing, and their quartiles would be shaky anyway.

choices.text: A violin, because it smooths the noise away
choices.why: With 20 values the smoothing mostly invents shape.

choices.text: A boxplot, because it is the most compact
choices.why: Compact is not honest: a box from 20 values claims precision it does not have.

choices.text: A pie of the deliveries by duration
choices.why: A pie is for part of a whole, not a distribution.

prompt: A violin plot shows a smooth single peak, but the strip of the same data shows a clear gap in the middle. What explains the difference?

choices.text: The strip invented the gap with its jitter
choices.why: Jitter moves dots across, never along the axis.

choices.text: The violin was drawn from a different sample
choices.why: Same data; the difference is the smoothing.

choices.text: Violins cannot show gaps at any setting
choices.why: With a small enough bandwidth they can.

choices.text: The bandwidth smoothed the gap away
choices.why: Right. A violin inherits the density curve's hidden setting.

prompt: In what order should five regional boxplots be drawn?

choices.text: In the order of the file
choices.why: That order means nothing to the reader.

choices.text: By median, slowest first
choices.why: Right. The ranking becomes the picture, as in lesson 3.

choices.text: Alphabetically by region name
choices.why: Alphabetical helps lookup, not comparison.

choices.text: By the number of outliers
choices.why: Outliers are not the main comparison.

prompt: The slowest median was 35.5 minutes and the fastest 30.8. How far apart are they, in minutes, to one decimal place?
Each region's middle half spans ten to fifteen minutes, and the medians differ by under five. What does that say?

choices.text: Variation inside regions outweighs the gaps between them
choices.why: Right. Every box overlaps every other.

choices.text: Centre-West has a delivery problem
choices.why: A five-minute gap inside heavily overlapping boxes does not show that.

choices.text: The data must be wrong
choices.why: This is the most common finding in any comparison of groups.

choices.text: The boxes should be drawn narrower
choices.why: Width does not change what the boxes say.

prompt: Somebody replaces the five boxplots with a bar chart of the five medians, from 35.5 to 30.8. What does the bar chart lose?

choices.text: Nothing, since the medians are the same
choices.why: The medians are; everything around them is gone.

choices.text: The order of the regions
choices.why: Bars can be sorted just as easily.

choices.text: The zero baseline
choices.why: A bar chart keeps its baseline at zero.

choices.text: The spread, so differences look certain
choices.why: Right. Five bars of different lengths invite a ranking the data does not support.

prompt: Find each part of this boxplot.

labels.text: the end of the upper whisker

hint: The median is the line inside the box.

prompt: Put the five numbers of the delivery boxplot in order, smallest first.
Match each chart to what it shows best.

pairs.right: five numbers to compare across groups
the shape, including a second peak
the summary and whether it is fair

right_distractors: the share of each group in the total

prompt: The limit one and a half box lengths beyond the box, past which values are drawn on their own, is called the ___.
A report shows boxplots of salaries by department, with no points and no counts. One department has 4 people. What is the main risk?

choices.text: Salaries cannot be shown as boxplots
choices.why: They can; the issue is the small group.

choices.text: Its median will be zero
choices.why: Four salaries have a median like any other group.

choices.text: The whiskers will be missing
choices.why: They will be drawn; the box will just mean little.

choices.text: Its box looks as solid as the others
choices.why: Right. Four values make quartiles that one hire could move.

prompt: Who introduced the boxplot?

choices.text: Jacques Bertin
choices.why: Bertin named the visual variables in lesson 1.

choices.text: William Cleveland
choices.why: Cleveland ranked the channels in lesson 2.

choices.text: S. S. Stevens
choices.why: Stevens measured how size is perceived, lesson 2.

choices.text: John Tukey
choices.why: Right, in the 1970s.
